case_study_insert.main_stem: Eastbridge Academy of Learning (EAL) is a private limited company in the education sector, running a vocational training college with a workforce of 80. Founded in 2015 by Helena Wu, the business operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. EAL plans to invest $480,000 in a new e-learning studio and digital learning platform, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $180,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $26 a unit and a selling price of $62, and currently produces 9,600 units a year. EAL faces two problems: student dropout has reached 12% and tutor absenteeism is rising sharply, disrupting live classes and learner support.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Enrolments Report - Q3 2025: The college enrolled 2,400 learners last quarter with a course pass rate of 78%, down from 86% a year ago. Student complaints fell from 52 to 29 per month. Average course-material dispatch time is 2.4 days. A survey of 400 prospective students found that 71% would pay $20 more for livestreamed tutorials and 63% check digital-platform quality before enrolling. A skills audit shows 24 of 80 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new e-learning platform; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Eastbridge Academy of Learning for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.9% from $13.25 to $13.90 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Education technology and printed-material input costs have risen 7.3% year-on-year, while consumer spending on adult education grew 2.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: EAL plans to fund part of its $480,000 e-learning expansion with a five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for EAL of using a share issue to raise the $180,000 instead of extra bank borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share capital does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $300,000 bank loan, so EAL's cash flow is protected while it absorbs fixed costs of $144,000 a year and a 7.3% rise in technology input costs. This strengthens the college's ability to reinvest in the digital platform.

Point 2: Equity spreads the risk of the new e-learning venture among shareholders rather than leaving Helena Wu's original backers exposed to loan covenants or repossession of the studio. It also enlarges the capital base supporting the $480,000 investment without increasing the interest payable already in Appendix 2.

Equity also matches the long payback of an e-learning platform: the $480,000 investment should lift the 42.0% gross margin over several years, so funding it with eight years of loan interest would mismatch the benefit stream. With dropout at 12%, a share issue leaves cash available for learner support and the $750 retraining without cutting the $144,000 fixed-cost budget or the 9,600-enrolment target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over bank borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to EAL's expansion, loan and cost data.

questions.question_text: EAL is launching its new e-learning platform. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing. Which should EAL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television: National TV gives EAL instant mass awareness of the digital platform across the country. Yet airtime is prohibitive for an 80-staff college funding a $480,000 expansion, and most viewers are not prospective vocational learners, so much of the budget is wasted.

Local radio: Regional radio is cheap and reaches EAL's local catchment quickly, ideal for a college that recruits nearby students. Its limit is reach: filling enough places to cover $144,000 of fixed costs and the 9,600-unit enrolment target needs more than one local audience.

Social media influencer marketing: Education and careers influencers reach exactly the 71% of 400 surveyed students who would pay $20 more for livestreamed tutorials and the 63% who check platform quality. Engagement is measurable and nationally scalable at low cost per lead, though results take time and depend on credibility.

With only 2,400 learners enrolled last quarter, EAL cannot afford a campaign whose cost is unrelated to enrolments; influencer fees can be tied to sign-ups and measured against the $36 contribution per place. Reach from television would be largely wasted on viewers outside the college's recruitment area, while radio's 2.4-day dispatch message cannot be shown visually; a targeted digital campaign fits the flat, 80-staff organisation and the $480,000 platform budget.

Recommendation: EAL should choose social media influencer marketing. It hits the exact survey segment, scales nationally like radio cannot, and costs far less than television. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow for the enrolment target, so EAL should add targeted school and careers-fair follow-up to convert the leads.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to EAL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of EAL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in EAL's context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: EAL's student dropout has reached 12% and tutor absenteeism is rising. Explain two benefits for EAL of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation among its tutors.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets EAL's experienced tutors design their own livestreamed tutorials, giving them autonomy and ownership that raise job satisfaction and help address the 12% dropout through more engaging, tutor-led delivery. In a flat structure of 80 staff this freedom suits skilled professionals.

Point 2: Delegating decisions speeds responses to learner problems without waiting for Helena Wu, helping cut the pass-rate decline from 86% to 78% and the rising absenteeism. Motivated tutors are likelier to stay, avoiding repeated $750 per employee retraining and protecting the 9,600-enrolment target.

Autonomy suits a flat college of 80 where tutors know their learners best; letting them redesign livestreamed tutorials can lift the 78% pass rate, which in turn supports the 71% willingness to pay $20 more found in the survey. Stable, motivated tutors also protect the $1,050,000 gross profit in 2025, since high turnover would force repeated $750 hiring and disrupt the 2,400 learners enrolled last quarter.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of laissez-faire leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to EAL's dropout, retention and output.

questions.question_text: EAL must upskill 24 tutors to use the new e-learning platform. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should EAL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching while tutors run real courses is specific to EAL's own platform, costs no fees and keeps all 24 tutors teaching, protecting the 2,400 learners enrolled last quarter and the 78% pass rate. However, mentor tutors lose preparation time, bad habits can spread and there is no external certificate.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee gives structured digital-skills training and a recognised certificate for 24 tutors, costing $18,000 - modest against the $480,000 investment. It removes tutors from teaching, risking the 12% dropout worsening, and generic modules may not match EAL's platform, so in-house follow-up would be needed.

The 24 untutored staff make up 30% of the 80-strong workforce, so removing them for a full college course would cut teaching capacity sharply and could worsen the 12% dropout at the moment the platform launches. On-the-job coaching spreads the $750-per-employee saving into learner support instead. EAL should still record competence checks so quality assurance is not sacrificed, and can fund short college modules from the 14.0% operating margin later if needed.

Decision: EAL should choose on-the-job training first, adding short college modules for lead tutors. It is cheaper, platform-specific and avoids losing teaching capacity while dropout is 12%; full off-the-job training is rejected because an $18,000 fee and 24 tutors away from class would disrupt learner support, and college sessions can be scheduled later once the platform stabilises.

The $18,000 college route would also consume a notable slice of the $480,000 platform budget for a single cohort, whereas on-the-job delivery can be repeated cheaply as new tutors join.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to EAL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in EAL's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in EAL's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and platform relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how EAL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $144,000 ÷ ($62 − $26) = $144,000 ÷ $36 = 4,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 4,000 enrolments a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $62 − $26 = $36. Answer: contribution per unit is $36.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways EAL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 4,000-unit break-even point with 9,600 actual enrolments, a margin of safety of 5,600 places, to judge whether the e-learning studio is fully subscribed.
2. Use $36 contribution to test a $10 discount to $52, leaving $26 per place, still above the $26 variable cost and helping lift the 78% pass-rate reputation with affordable fees.
3. Set enrolment targets that service the $300,000 bank loan and justify the $480,000 platform spend before Helena Wu commits further capital.
4. Monitor average total cost of $41.0 ($144,000 ÷ 9,600 + $26) each term to detect waste and to judge whether the 7.3% technology-cost rise is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 4,000 enrolments | (ii) Contribution per unit = $36 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety vs 9,600 enrolments; discount modelling vs $144,000 fixed costs; loan servicing for the $480,000 platform; and average total cost of $41.0 to track cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid, contextual use in (iii) (max 4).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EAL's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has EAL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 38.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 11.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 22.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $760,000 on revenue of $2,000,000 is 38.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $1,050,000 on revenue of $2,500,000 is 42.0%. Operating profit of $220,000 in 2024 equals 11.0% of revenue and 22.0% of the $1,000,000 capital employed; in 2025 operating profit of $350,000 is 14.0% of revenue and 25.0% of the $1,400,000 capital employed. Cost of sales rose from $1,240,000 to $1,450,000 but more slowly than revenue.

Evaluation: Every measure improved. Gross margins widened from 38.0% to 42.0%, reflecting better control of teaching and technology costs; operating margins rose from 11.0% to 14.0%, so more of each fee dollar becomes operating profit; and returns on capital employed increased from 22.0% to 25.0%, showing the enlarged asset base is still productive. Interest payable rose from $25,000 to $35,000, a growing but small burden, and the 7.3% technology-cost rise could erode the gross-margin gain if fees stay flat.

Interest payable of $35,000 remains small beside $350,000 operating profit, so debt service does not negate the gain, though the 7.3% technology-cost rise requires monitoring to protect the enlarged 42.0% margin.

Conclusion: EAL's financial position has improved on all three measures, and because margins and capital returns both rose the gain is not just a revenue effect. The main risk is rising interest and input costs, so management should defend the 42.0% gross margin before the $480,000 e-learning investment adds more capital.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of margin, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for EAL of offering the $20 livestreamed-tutorial premium identified in its survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Of 400 prospective students surveyed, 71% would pay $20 more for livestreamed tutorials and 63% check platform quality, so the premium lifts fee revenue per enrolment and protects the $36 contribution even as technology costs rise 7.3%. It also supports the new e-learning platform's positioning and the 78% pass rate.

Disadvantage: Price-sensitive learners may reject the $20 premium and cut the 9,600 enrolments needed to justify the $480,000 studio, worsening the 12% dropout. Delivering live streams may also distract tutors and raise absenteeism, undermining the platform's quality signal to the 63% who check it.

EAL should pilot the $20 premium on one livestreamed course and compare enrolment with a control group, because the 63% who check platform quality may expect visible improvements in return. Discrimination is a risk: learners unable to pay could be excluded, worsening the 12% dropout and conflicting with the college's educational aim. Any premium revenue should be reinvested in the platform so the 42.0% gross margin is defended rather than merely harvested.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to EAL's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 7.3% rise in education input costs will affect EAL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If EAL's $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year, small beside $144,000 of fixed costs; a fixed loan means zero direct effect. Higher rates may deter learners financing fees, and EAL can cap the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $13.90 an hour): With a workforce of 80, some support and administrative roles are hourly-paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or pay rates, so no annual figure can be invented; the sound test is productivity - 9,600 enrolments ÷ 80 staff = 120 places per worker - meaning the rise is absorbable only while that productivity holds, or the $36 contribution shrinks.

Input cost inflation (7.3%): The $26 variable cost per enrolment covers materials and platform delivery, but the insert does not split it, so only a bound is valid: a full 7.3% rise is 0.073 × $26 = $1.90 per place, or about $18,200 a year at 9,600 enrolments (9,600 × $1.90). Even a partial rise cuts contribution, and the $20 premium can offset only part.

Conclusion: The 7.3% rise in education input costs has the greatest impact because it touches all 9,600 enrolments and directly erodes the $36 contribution funding the $480,000 platform; the wage rise is manageable at 120 places per worker, and the interest rise costs at most $2,250 and can be fixed, so neither matches the input-cost shock.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to EAL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on EAL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in EAL's context with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
